apmo-1989-01.title: Compare symmetric sums term by term
apmo-1989-01.body:
Let $\sigma_k$ be the $k$-th elementary symmetric sum of $x_1,\dots,x_n$, i.e. the sum of all products $x_{i_1}x_{i_2}\cdots x_{i_k}$ with $i_1<i_2<\dots<i_k$. Expanding the product gives
$$(1+x_1)(1+x_2)\cdots(1+x_n)=1+\sigma_1+\sigma_2+\cdots+\sigma_n .$$
So it suffices to show $\sigma_k\le \dfrac{S^k}{k!}$ for each $k=1,\dots,n$.

Write $S^k=(x_1+\dots+x_n)(x_1+\dots+x_n)\cdots(x_1+\dots+x_n)$ ($k$ factors) and expand: we get the sum of $x_{j_1}x_{j_2}\cdots x_{j_k}$ over all $n^k$ sequences $(j_1,\dots,j_k)$, every term positive. Fix a set $\{i_1,\dots,i_k\}$ of $k$ distinct indices. Each of the $k!$ orderings of this set is a different sequence $(j_1,\dots,j_k)$ and contributes the term $x_{i_1}\cdots x_{i_k}$. Hence the expansion of $S^k$ contains every term of $\sigma_k$ at least $k!$ times (and further positive terms), so
$$S^k\ge k!\,\sigma_k .$$
Summing $\sigma_k\le S^k/k!$ over $k=1,\dots,n$ and adding $1$ gives the inequality. ∎

apmo-1989-01.title: AM-GM and the binomial theorem
apmo-1989-01.body:
By AM-GM applied to the $n$ positive numbers $1+x_i$,
$$\prod_{i=1}^n(1+x_i)\le\left(\frac{(1+x_1)+\dots+(1+x_n)}{n}\right)^n=\left(1+\frac Sn\right)^n .$$
By the binomial theorem,
$$\left(1+\frac Sn\right)^n=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk\frac{S^k}{n^k}=\sum_{k=0}^n\frac{S^k}{k!}\cdot\frac{n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)}{n^k}\le\sum_{k=0}^n\frac{S^k}{k!},$$
because $n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)\le n^k$. Combining the two inequalities proves the claim. ∎

apmo-1989-02.title: Infinite descent
apmo-1989-02.body:
Changing signs does not matter, so suppose there is a solution in non-negative integers other than $(0,0,0,0)$ and choose one with $a+b+c+n>0$ as small as possible. We show that $a,b,c,n$ are all even; then $(a/2,b/2,c/2,n/2)$ is again a solution (divide the equation by $4$), not all zero, with smaller sum — a contradiction.

**Step 1.** $6\mid 5n^2$, so $2\mid n$ and $3\mid n$; write $n=6n_0$. The equation becomes $6a^2+3b^2+c^2=30n_0^2$. Then $3\mid c^2$, so $c=3c_0$, and dividing by $3$:
$$2a^2+b^2+3c_0^2=10n_0^2. \tag{1}$$

**Step 2: $b$ and $c_0$ are even.** From (1), $b^2+3c_0^2$ is even, so $b\equiv c_0\pmod 2$. Squares are $0$ or $1$ mod $4$, so in either case $b^2+3c_0^2\equiv 0\pmod 4$. Then $2(5n_0^2-a^2)\equiv0\pmod 4$, so $5n_0^2-a^2$ is even and $a\equiv n_0\pmod 2$. Hence $n_0-a$ and $n_0+a$ are both even and $n_0^2-a^2\equiv0\pmod 4$. Reducing (1) modulo $8$ (using $10n_0^2\equiv 2n_0^2$):
$$b^2+3c_0^2\equiv 2(n_0^2-a^2)\equiv 0\pmod 8.$$
If $b,c_0$ were both odd we would get $b^2+3c_0^2\equiv1+3=4\pmod 8$ (odd squares are $1$ mod $8$). So $b=2b_0$ and $c_0=2c_1$, and (1) becomes
$$a^2+2b_0^2+6c_1^2=5n_0^2. \tag{2}$$

**Step 3: $a$ and $n_0$ are even.** The same argument applies to (2). Modulo $8$ it reads $a^2+3n_0^2\equiv 2(c_1^2-b_0^2)\pmod 8$. The left side is even, so $a\equiv n_0\pmod 2$, hence $a^2+3n_0^2\equiv0\pmod 4$; then $c_1^2-b_0^2$ is even, so $c_1\equiv b_0\pmod2$ and $c_1^2-b_0^2\equiv0\pmod4$. Therefore $a^2+3n_0^2\equiv0\pmod8$, which rules out $a,n_0$ both odd. So $a$ and $n_0$ are even.

**Conclusion.** $a$ is even, $b=2b_0$ is even, $c=3c_0=6c_1$ is even and $n=6n_0$ is even, which gives the contradiction described above. Hence the only integer solution is $a=b=c=n=0$. ∎

apmo-1989-03.title: Vectors from the centroid
apmo-1989-03.body:
Put the origin at the centroid $G$ of triangle $A_1A_2A_3$, so $A_1+A_2+A_3=0$ (indices mod $3$); any two of the vectors $A_1,A_2,A_3$ are linearly independent. Then
$$B_n=\frac{A_n+A_{n+1}}2=-\frac{A_{n+2}}2,\qquad C_n=\frac{A_n+B_n}{2}=\frac{A_n}{2}-\frac{A_{n+2}}{4}.$$

**The points $D_n$.** The line $B_nA_{n+2}$ is the median through $A_{n+2}$ (it passes through $0$), so $D_n=\lambda A_{n+2}=-\lambda A_n-\lambda A_{n+1}$. Also $C_{n+1}=\frac{A_{n+1}}2-\frac{A_n}4$, and a point of line $A_nC_{n+1}$ is
$$A_n+t(C_{n+1}-A_n)=\Big(1-\tfrac{5t}{4}\Big)A_n+\tfrac t2A_{n+1}.$$
Comparing coefficients: $\frac t2=-\lambda$ and $1-\frac{5t}4=-\lambda$, so $t=\frac47$ and $\lambda=-\frac27$. Thus $D_n=-\frac27A_{n+2}$: triangle $D_1D_2D_3$ is the image of $A_1A_2A_3$ under the homothety with centre $G$ and ratio $-\frac27$.

**The points $E_n$.** $B_{n+1}=-\frac{A_n}2$, so the line $A_nB_{n+1}$ is the median through $A_n$ and $E_n=\mu A_n$. A point of line $C_nA_{n+2}$ is
$$A_{n+2}+s(C_n-A_{n+2})=\tfrac s2A_n+\Big(1-\tfrac{5s}4\Big)A_{n+2}.$$
For this to be a multiple of $A_n$ we need $s=\frac45$, giving $\mu=\frac25$. So $E_n=\frac25A_n$, and $E_1E_2E_3$ is the image of $A_1A_2A_3$ under the homothety with centre $G$ and ratio $\frac25$.

**Areas.** $[D_1D_2D_3]=\frac4{49}[A_1A_2A_3]$ and $[E_1E_2E_3]=\frac4{25}[A_1A_2A_3]$, so
$$\frac{[D_1D_2D_3]}{[E_1E_2E_3]}=\frac{4/49}{4/25}=\frac{25}{49}.$$
**Answer: $\dfrac{25}{49}$**

apmo-1989-03.title: Menelaus on the medians
apmo-1989-03.body:
Let $G$ be the centroid; the medians are $A_1B_2$, $A_2B_3$, $A_3B_1$ ($B_2$ is the midpoint of $A_2A_3$, etc.).

**$D_1$.** $D_1$ lies on the median $A_3B_1$. Apply Menelaus to triangle $B_1A_2A_3$ and the line through $A_1$, $D_1$, $C_2$ ($C_2$ on $A_2A_3$ with $A_2C_2=\frac14A_2A_3$, $A_1$ on line $A_2B_1$ with $A_1B_1=B_1A_2$):
$$\frac{B_1A_1}{A_1A_2}\cdot\frac{A_2C_2}{C_2A_3}\cdot\frac{A_3D_1}{D_1B_1}=1\ \Longrightarrow\ \frac12\cdot\frac13\cdot\frac{A_3D_1}{D_1B_1}=1,$$
so $A_3D_1:D_1B_1=6:1$. With $A_3B_1=21t$ we get $D_1B_1=3t$ and $A_3G=14t$, $GB_1=7t$, so $D_1$ is on segment $GB_1$ with $GD_1=4t=\frac27GA_3$, on the opposite side of $G$ from $A_3$. By symmetry $D_n$ is the image of $A_{n+2}$ under the homothety with centre $G$, ratio $-\frac27$.

**$E_1$.** $E_1$ lies on the median $A_1B_2$. Menelaus in triangle $A_1A_2B_2$ with the line through $C_1$, $E_1$, $A_3$ ($C_1$ on $A_1A_2$ with $A_1C_1=\frac14A_1A_2$; $A_3$ on line $A_2B_2$ with $B_2A_3=\frac12A_2A_3$):
$$\frac{A_1C_1}{C_1A_2}\cdot\frac{A_2A_3}{A_3B_2}\cdot\frac{B_2E_1}{E_1A_1}=1\ \Longrightarrow\ \frac13\cdot 2\cdot\frac{B_2E_1}{E_1A_1}=1,$$
so $A_1E_1:E_1B_2=2:3$, i.e. $A_1E_1=\frac25A_1B_2$. With $A_1B_2=15u$: $A_1G=10u$, $A_1E_1=6u$, $GE_1=4u=\frac25GA_1$, on the same side as $A_1$. So $E_n$ is the image of $A_n$ under the homothety with centre $G$, ratio $\frac25$.

Hence the ratio of areas is $\left(\frac{2/7}{2/5}\right)^2=\frac{25}{49}$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{25}{49}$**

apmo-1989-04.title: Count common partners, then Cauchy–Schwarz
apmo-1989-04.body:
Think of $S$ as a graph on the vertices $1,\dots,n$: each pair $(a,b)\in S$ is an edge. A triple $(a,b,c)$ with $(a,b),(a,c),(b,c)\in S$ (so $a<b<c$) is a triangle of this graph; let $T$ be the number of such triples.

For each $i$ let $D_i$ be the set of numbers paired with $i$ in $S$ and $d_i=|D_i|$. Since each pair contains two numbers,
$$\sum_{i=1}^n d_i=2m.$$

**Triangles on one edge.** Take a pair $\{i,j\}\in S$. Any $k\in D_i\cap D_j$ is different from $i$ and $j$ (no number is paired with itself), and $\{i,j,k\}$ is a triangle. Since $D_i\cup D_j\subseteq\{1,\dots,n\}$,
$$|D_i\cap D_j|=d_i+d_j-|D_i\cup D_j|\ge d_i+d_j-n .$$
So the edge $\{i,j\}$ lies in at least $d_i+d_j-n$ triangles.

**Summing.** Each triangle has three edges, so summing over all $m$ edges counts every triangle exactly three times:
$$3T=\sum_{\{i,j\}\in S}|D_i\cap D_j|\ge\sum_{\{i,j\}\in S}(d_i+d_j-n).$$
In $\sum_{\{i,j\}\in S}(d_i+d_j)$ the number $d_i$ appears once for every edge containing $i$, i.e. $d_i$ times, so this sum is $\sum_i d_i^2$. Hence
$$3T\ge\sum_{i=1}^n d_i^2-mn\ge\frac{\left(\sum_i d_i\right)^2}{n}-mn=\frac{4m^2}{n}-mn,$$
using the Cauchy–Schwarz (or QM-AM) inequality $\sum d_i^2\ge\frac1n\left(\sum d_i\right)^2$. Therefore
$$T\ge\frac13\left(\frac{4m^2}{n}-mn\right)=\frac{4m\left(m-\frac{n^2}{4}\right)}{3n}. \qquad ∎$$

apmo-1989-05.title: Iterate and use monotonicity
apmo-1989-05.body:
**These work.** If $f(x)=x+c$, then $f$ is strictly increasing, $g(x)=x-c$, and $f(x)+g(x)=2x$.

**No others.** Let $f$ satisfy the conditions and write $f^n$ for the $n$-th iterate ($f^0(x)=x$).

*Arithmetic progression.* Put $f^{n+1}(x)$ into condition 2. Since $g(f^{n+1}(x))=f^n(x)$,
$$f^{n+2}(x)+f^n(x)=2f^{n+1}(x),\quad\text{i.e.}\quad f^{n+2}(x)-f^{n+1}(x)=f^{n+1}(x)-f^n(x).$$
So the differences $f^{k+1}(x)-f^k(x)$ are all equal to $f(x)-x=:\varphi(x)$, and summing,
$$f^n(x)=x+n\varphi(x)\qquad(n\ge0).$$
Condition 2 is symmetric in $f$ and $g$ ($g$ is the inverse of $f$ and $f$ the inverse of $g$), so likewise $g^n(x)=x+n(g(x)-x)=x-n\varphi(x)$, because $g(x)-x=x-f(x)$.

*Monotonicity.* $g$ is strictly increasing: if $g(x)\ge g(y)$ then $x=f(g(x))\ge f(g(y))=y$. Compositions of strictly increasing functions are strictly increasing, so all $f^n$ and $g^n$ are.

Now take $x>y$ and $n\ge1$. From $f^n(x)>f^n(y)$ and $g^n(x)>g^n(y)$:
$$x+n\varphi(x)>y+n\varphi(y)\ \Rightarrow\ n(\varphi(x)-\varphi(y))>-(x-y),$$
$$x-n\varphi(x)>y-n\varphi(y)\ \Rightarrow\ n(\varphi(x)-\varphi(y))<x-y.$$
So $n\,|\varphi(x)-\varphi(y)|<x-y$ for every positive integer $n$, which forces $\varphi(x)=\varphi(y)$. Thus $\varphi$ is a constant $c$, i.e. $f(x)=x+c$.

**Answer:** $f(x)=x+c$ for any real constant $c$. ∎
